{\Large\bfseries Progressive Proof Practice}\par
MATH 147 $|$ Lectures 7--8\par\medskip
Questions arranged by lecture. L1 = basics, L2 = standard theorem, L3 = application, L4 = challenge. CORE marks priority questions.

\lecture{7}{27--30}{Convergence \& Divergence}
\q{1}{Uniqueness Lemma}{L1}
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that if $|a - b| < \varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, then $a = b$.
\q{2}{Uniqueness of Limits}{L2 \quad CORE}
Prove that a sequence of real numbers has at most one limit.
\q{3}{A Non-Cauchy Sequence}{L2}
Prove directly from the definition that
\[ x_n = 1 + (-1)^n \]
is not Cauchy.
\newpage
\lecture{8}{31--32}{Algebra of Limits}
\q{4}{Direct Limit Proof}{L1}
Prove directly from the definition that
\[ \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{4n+3}{n+1} = 4. \]
\q{5}{Euler's Number}{L3}
Let
\[ a_n = \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n. \]
Prove that $\{a_n\}$ is increasing and bounded above by 3.
\q{6}{Infinite Limit Application}{L4 \quad CORE}
Let $x_n = n^2/(1-n)$ for $n \geq 2$. Prove directly that $x_n \to -\infty$.
